items.title: 67426_Hayes Pillars oral history interview
items.q: We had a chance to fraternize with Duke, the boys in the band.

ctx.x: They drew big crowds for a while, but by late summer, they had died down. So they tried to go in for cheaper acts, see. And they just didn't get it. And business just started dying down. And in the following year, 1945, they went out of business. Went out of business.

But when they just had that lower budget, see, they were able to sustain -- you know what I mean -- a little loss here, and a little loss there, you know what I mean, see, and just keep going. That's what's happened. And we stayed at the Club Riviera all through that year, and we drew people, see. And things got a little dead just before Christmas. Our contract ran out on the tenth of January. The following weekend, we opened at the Rum Boogie in Chicago. This was in 1945. We opened at the Rum Boogie, and the…

That's how great a tone he had. He could sing through anything. The man just had -- he was just a great alto saxophone player. Now, he was no virtuoso, also, see, but he had that tone. And you had -- he was a slow reader, and that -- he always was that. He never did improve too much on this. But once he got something, he had it, man, he could lead that section. My brother Charles would tell you the same thing. He was something to hear.
